resources.description: This provides an opportunity for students to consider how the sine and cosine functions behave in a "which is bigger?" context. Working on this problem could help to reinforce students' understanding of the behaviour of trigonometric functions and the problem can be attempted in a variety of different ways.

resources.title: Equation or identity? (I)
resources.description: Here students consider some trigonometric equations in the context of triangles only, deciding whether any of these is in fact an identity. This should help to reinforce the distinction between equations and identities. There are plenty of opportunities for students try to justify their decisions, prove identities and find counter examples.

resources.title: Have a sine
resources.description: Students express several lengths in a unit circle diagram using trigonometric functions and thereby develop their understanding of how trigonometric functions are related to each other. This problem is accessible to any student with a basic understanding of trigonometry in right-angled triangles and offers opportunities to discuss what happens if $\theta$ varies.  There is also a historical link with names for expressions such as $\tfrac{1}{2}(1-\cos \theta).$

resources.description: This offers an opportunity to apply some basic trigonometry to a situation that students start by visualising. Asking students to explain why their solutions work for all angles from $0$ to $2\pi$ could help to make links with graphs of trigonometric functions and how these relate to the original situation.
